draft.title: German Australians in wartime
card: When war began in 1914, Australia was at war with Germany. Many Australians of German background, including people born in Australia, came under suspicion.
The War Precautions Act gave the government wide powers in wartime. It was used to restrict the freedom of people seen as a danger to the war effort.
Thousands of people of German background were interned, which means held in camps without a trial. Some were also made to report to police or lost their jobs.
Many German place names were changed to English ones, such as Hahndorf in South Australia, which became Ambleside. Some German schools and clubs were closed.
draft.remember: Fear of the enemy led to loss of freedom for people of German background, even those born in Australia.

a.q: Why were many German Australians interned during the First World War?
opts: The government treated their background as a possible danger
They had broken the law by refusing to enlist
They had asked to be kept safe from attacks
They were prisoners captured in battle overseas
a.why: Australia was at war with Germany, so people of German background came under suspicion and the War Precautions Act let the government restrict them. Most had not been captured in battle, and being interned was not a choice for their own safety.
a.clue: Think about who Australia was fighting and what the Act allowed.

b.q: In 1916, a town council in South Australia votes to replace its German name with an English one. What does this show about the home front?
opts: Anti-German feeling reached daily life in Australian towns
Most towns were being moved to new sites away from the coast
Germany had taken control of local councils in Australia
The government wanted to attract more settlers to the town
b.why: Renaming towns was one way anti-German feeling showed in daily life during the war. It was not about moving towns or about Germany controlling councils, and the change did not aim to attract settlers.
b.clue: Ask what a name change tells you about how people felt about Germany.

a.best: The government treated their background as a possible danger

b.best: Anti-German feeling reached daily life in Australian towns

problems.detail: The scenario has a South Australian town council voting in 1916 to rename the town. Most South Australian renamings, including Hahndorf to Ambleside, were made in 1918 under the state's Nomenclature Act 1917, not by council votes. A hypothetical case is fine, but 'a town in Victoria' or 'in 1918, South Australia renamed a town' would fit the record better.
